coach_says: Your knight on d4 was only protected by the queen on d1, and Bd3 stands right in the way of that protection. Now ...Nxd4 simply wins a piece. Before you put a piece on a file or diagonal, check whether it cuts off a defender. Nxc6 first (or f3 to hold e4) kept everything protected.
concept: blocked the queen's defence of d4

coach_says: Pushing to c2 looks scary, but after Rc1 the pawn is stuck and White's knight comes to e3 to win it. Rc5 was much better: it hits the knight, takes your rook off c8 where Ne7+ forked it, and keeps the c3 pawn protected from behind while your queenside pawns get going. A passed pawn is only strong while it is supported; don't rush it to a square where it can be blockaded and picked off.

Your e5 pawn was attacked by the knight on f3 and nothing defended it, so after Bc5 White just takes it with Nxe5. Before you develop, check whether any of your pieces or pawns are under attack. Nc6 develops and protects e5 at the same time.

White's king is stuck in the centre with broken kingside pawns and almost nothing developed, so every move counts. b5 is a slow pawn move that does nothing to that king. Bring pieces in instead: Qh4+ chases the king, Nc6 hits d4 and b4, and Rg8 uses the open g-file.
concept: slow pawn move instead of attacking

coach_says: Your rook on d3 was attacked by the king, but White's bishop on c6 was also loose, attacked by your rook on c8 and defended by nothing. Instead of retreating, Rxd2+ gives the doomed rook for a bishop with check, and then Rxc6 takes the second bishop. When one of your pieces is going to be lost anyway, look for what it can take on the way out, ideally with check.

Your knight had to move, but on c5 it is simply kicked by ...b6 and has to go to the edge on a6. Ne5 was the square: it attacks the c4 pawn and f7, and Black's dangerous c-pawn soon drops. Put your knight where it hits weak pawns and can't just be chased away.

Black's king is still in the middle on an open e-file, so Re1+ first is strong: Black has to block awkwardly, and then your bishop goes to b5 with a pin on c6. Bd3 lets Black develop in peace and blocks your d-pawn and c1 bishop. When the e-file opens and the enemy king hasn't castled, look for the rook check before retreating.
concept: use the open e-file with check

coach_says: After Bxe5 fxe5, the pawn attacks your knight on f6, and that knight was guarding d5, which is hit by Bb3 and Rd1. When the f6 knight moves, White wins material on d5. Before trading, check what the recapture attacks; Rad8 instead adds a defender to d5 and keeps your bishop.
concept: recapture hits the d5 knight's defender

coach_says: Your knight on g5 was attacked by h6, so the simple answer was to retreat it with Nf3. Bh7+ Kh8 just forces your bishop to go back to d3, and Black then plays ...Nb4 to swap it off while you have lost time. A check is only good if it gains something; ask what the position looks like after the king steps aside.
Good move. d5 attacks your opponent's bishop on c4 while they spend a move taking your bishop on b1, so you get something back. That is the engine's choice too.
Nc6 is about as good as anything here. You are a piece down and the engine's top choices are all close, so there is no clear lesson in this move.
Be2 is fine: it breaks the pin on the f3 knight so you can win the d4 pawn. Bc4 was very slightly better, but the difference is tiny.
Kd3 is fine and you are still winning. Bringing the king towards the centre and the queenside pawns is the right plan in this endgame.

The knight on e5 was attacking your bishop on c4. f4 attacks the knight back, but it just takes your bishop with Nxc4, so you lose your strong light-squared bishop and the bishop pair. You are a piece up for pawns, and keeping your bishops makes that piece count. Retreat with Bb3 first, then play f4 later.
concept: let the knight trade off your bishop

coach_says: Your bishop on d2 was attacked by the rook on d8, and your bishop on c6 and knight on b5 were loose. Rd1 saves d2, but ...Rb6 then hits both c6 and b5 and Black wins material back. Nd4 was the move: it blocks the d-file, protects c6, and is itself protected by e3. Look for one move that covers several loose pieces.
concept: loose pieces on b5 and c6
also: block the file with a defending piece

coach_says: Your f5 pawn was blocking White's bishop on c2 from reaching h7. Pushing f4 opens that diagonal, and Qe4 attacks both your rook on a8 and h7 with mate ideas. You have to defend with ...Nf6 and then White takes the f4 pawn. Before moving a pawn, check which lines it opens towards your own king.

Your e5 pawn was attacked twice, by the d4 pawn and the knight on f3, and d5 does nothing for it, so White takes it for free. Deal with the attacked pawn first: e4 pushes it forward with a gain of time, or exd4 trades it.

Black's bishop on g4 had just taken your knight and was attacking your queen on d1. Bxd6 ignores that, and Black simply takes your queen. When your queen is attacked, deal with it first: Qxg4 takes the bishop back and the material is level.
concept: missed the attack on your queen

coach_says: White's queen on e4 and bishop on c2 are lined up at h7, threatening Qxh7+ and a mating attack. Nb6 protects the a8 rook but leaves h7 undefended, and White mates with Qxh7+, Qh5+, Bh7+, Bg6+ and Qh7. Nf6 was the only move: it covers h7 and attacks the queen. When the enemy queen and bishop point at your king, check that first, before saving a rook.
concept: missed the mate threat on h7

coach_says: Black has pushed ...h6 and ...g5 without castling, and f4 is the way to punish that: it hits g5 and opens the f-file towards the king. Qf3 lets Black answer ...Ne5 with tempo on your queen, and then ...Bxd5 swaps off your good bishop. When the opponent overextends kingside pawns, look for the pawn break that attacks them.
concept: pawn break against the g5 pawn
